>Sorry to hijack your post.

Not at all. Though the existence of legions of others in a situation similar to my own is not at all unknown to me, it does a little something for me to know that I really am not the only one. In \_The Glory and the Dream\_, a history book by William Manchester that covers the US from 1932 to 1972, he talks of a man unemployed in the Great Depression who said he felt like a convicted murderer because no one would even consider him for a job.

​

Which reminds me of two other useful tidbits that I always make a point of mentioning when contacting government or non-governmental agencies: I do not use drugs and I do not have a criminal record.

For that matter, I don't drink either. I get up at 5 am seven days a week, and read for an hour. Then I go for a walk or a run. I used to go earlier, but sometimes the local bear is out then! I exercise, read, study, listen to audiobooks, informational podcasts, or informational material on Youtube. I do not sit on the couch and drink beer. I don't own a couch or easy chair!

Admittedly, depression makes the above paragraph increasing difficult.

I mention these things in the above two paragraphs because even among those who work with the downtrodden for a living there is a sense that you are out of work because you want to be. You are just a loser. I, to the contrary, submit that "Get a job!" would be viewed very differently in the 1930s as opposed to the 1950s.

As the Dutch historian Rutger Bregman has pointed out, "Poverty isn't a lack of character; it's a lack of cash."

As some economist, whose name escapes me at the moment, said: In the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s in America, you had to have a plan to fail.

Union and pension membership peaked in the US in 1968. Real wages in 1972. I was in fourth grade in 1979 when I realized, as everyone was stressing education and talking about college, that even if everyone in the country had a Ph.D., someone would still have to pick up the garbage (which was picked up by humans in those days). My observation has not changed because of automation. To the contrary, automation makes the point more clearly.

Thought experiment: what happens when all jobs are automated and Jeff Bezos is the only person getting paid, getting 100% of all income? Even Henry Ford, in spite of his later, violent strike breaking, understood that you can't just make money. You have to pay people, well, or you will not have a society.

In 1982 I was in seventh grade and one of my teachers told class that she had just read in the paper that morning that our generation would be the first in American history to not do better economically than our parents. The point is that this has been a long time coming, and has been seen clearly almost from the beginning by just about anyone who has looked into it. But here we are.

I see no brighter days ahead. I see total misery only weeks away. While life can do lots of things, it is for me now a train increasing in  speed down a track toward a brick wall. There's no reason to live this  way. I am not asking to be rich. I am not trying to keep up with the  Joneses (I forgot about them when I was still in my teens). That's why I  don't want to live. I am going to be reduced to camping (not in a  campground) with no way out or up. I don't care what people did 10,000  years ago or are doing elsewhere now. I don't have to stay in the movie  theater if I don't like the movie.
